1:
The date is fixed by the feast it follows, and the week is reconstructed differently. Gill puts the twenty-fourth two days after tabernacles ended; Keil and Delitzsch make the twenty-second the feast's closing assembly and re-gather the congregation two days later. Clarke lays out the month: trumpets on the first, tabernacles from the fourteenth to the twenty-second, the separation from illegitimate wives on the twenty-third, the fast on the twenty-fourth. Ellicott marks only "one day of rest" between. Wesley supplies the psychology: consciences awakened, hearts filled with a grief the season of public joy did not allow them to express. Henry states the principle — the joy of our holy feasts must give way to the sorrow of our solemn fasts, "every thing" being "beautiful in its season" — and notes that at Nehemiah 8:9 they were restrained from weeping and are now directed to weep. He measures the day against Isaiah 58:5: a fast that men appointed, but such a fast as God had chosen, both a day to afflict the soul and a day to loose the bands of wickedness — "without this, spreading sackcloth and ashes under us is but a jest."

What the separation of verse 2 amounted to is disputed. Gill takes it of Israelites who had married Gentile wives, undiscovered in Ezra's reformation or contracted since, now putting them away as "a proof of the truth of their repentance." Clarke allows either, that more were found out or that those already separated had taken their wives back. Wesley widens it to all unnecessary society with the heathen, and Henry further, to the strange children as well as the strange wives: those who intend to join themselves to God by covenant must separate themselves from sin and sinners. Keil and Delitzsch deny the marital reference outright: it relates neither to dissolving heathen marriages nor, against Bertheau, to who was admitted, but was "a voluntary renunciation of connection with the heathen, and of heathen customs." Ellicott reads the word rather than the act, finding a deep propriety in the change to "seed".

The fourth parts are counted two ways. Keil and Delitzsch and Henry make each about three hours, six in all; Henry then reports Bishop Patrick's view that all twelve hours were so spent, reading from six to nine and twelve to three, praying in the intervening watches. Clarke, following Calmet, divides the daylight into four stretches and the exercises into three: hearing the law standing, prostration and confession, rising to praise. Wesley has them begin after the morning sacrifice and continue to the evening. Henry draws out the reciprocity: the word read furnishes matter for prayer, and prayer makes the word more profitable, since in the glass of the law we see our deformities. "Fasting without prayer is a body without a soul, a worthless carcase."

The two lists of Levites at verses 4 and 5 are read as a puzzle. Henry offers successive prayer, one by one, after the rule of 1 Corinthians 14:31, or else eight separate congregations each presided over by a Levite; Wesley takes the second, the congregation allotted between several pulpits. Keil and Delitzsch, noting five of the eight names recur, make the repetition mark two acts by the same men: crying to God themselves, then calling the people to worship. Ellicott finds the seam in the pronoun: it is "their God" in verse 4 and "your God" in verse 5, so these eight offered a prayer which is not inserted. He notes too that the Septuagint drops every name after Kadmiel and inserts "and Ezra said" before verse 6, and thinks the psalm perhaps Ezra's, uttered by the Levites for the congregation. Clarke takes the summons to stand as a rebuke to his own century, protesting "the shameless custom of many congregations of people to sit still while they profess to bless and praise God."
6:
Henry reads the opening adoration as four articles: the only living and true God; the Creator, so that "the first article of our creed is fitly made the first article of our praises"; the Protector, whose providence "extends itself to the highest beings, for they need it, and to the meanest, for they are not slighted by it"; and the object of the creatures' praises, exalted above not our blessing merely but all blessing — "put all the praises of heaven and earth together, and the thousandth part is not said of what might and should be said of the glory of God." Keil and Delitzsch show the rhetoric doing that work: heaven is enlarged by "heaven of heavens" as at Deuteronomy 10:14, earth by "the sea and all therein", while "all their host" belongs only to the heaven clause.

Who that host is divides them. Clarke renders strictly — not "preservest" but "thou givest life to them all", the host "prostrate themselves unto thee" — and cannot resist the parallel: "how near is this to the opinion of Kepler, that all the heavenly host are instinct with life, and navigate the great expanse on pinions adjusted to their respective orbits!" He then withdraws it: to preserve in being is a good sense of the word and does not necessarily imply vitality. Ellicott takes the worshippers for angels rather than stars, citing Psalms 103:21, and finds the verse's comprehensiveness reproduced only at Hebrews 1:3; Henry likewise reads "the world of holy angels".

On Abraham the question is what "foundest his heart faithful" reports. Gill points to the trial, faith appearing when Abraham offered up his son; Henry will not let the finding be a discovery — God found the heart faithful "because he made it so (for faith is not of ourselves, it is the gift of God)". Ellicott, counting the nations of the grant, notes only that "the Hivites are for some reason omitted."

Keil and Delitzsch untangle verse 9, which compresses two occasions afterwards expanded: the affliction God saw in Egypt, answered by the signs upon Pharaoh, and the cry at the Red Sea, answered by the dividing of the water. Gill insists God was "not a mere spectator" but looked with pity and sent a deliverer. Henry notes how seasonable the memory was to men interceding for a second deliverance out of Babylon, and Ellicott sends the reader to the Song of Moses to "mark in the Hebrew both the identity and the variation." Of the pillar Henry says it settled not the route only but the timetable, directing when they should remove and when and where rest, "all their stages and all their steps."

At Sinai the stress falls on the adjectives. Ellicott observes that five of the names given to the law in Psalm 119 are gathered here and applied first to the Sinaitic legislation and then to the later ordinances, but that the weight rests on "right", "true" and "good" as belonging rather to the Decalogue's eternal principles. Henry and Wesley ground the same words in natural equity and extend the goodness to the ceremonial institutions as tokens of God's kindness and types of gospel grace; Henry adds that the Lawgiver did not send only but came down himself. The sabbath clause is read three ways: Gill as peculiar to Israel and typical of the rest in Christ; Clarke as a restoration, since they had forgotten this first of all the commandments during the sojourn in Egypt; Ellicott as pointing forward, its prominence marking its weight in the covenant of the next chapter and throughout the book. Of the manna Ellicott notes a change of phrase "which our Lord consecrated for ever" at John 6; Henry sums the wilderness provision as food convenient in the way and the good land at journey's end — "what would they more?"
16:
Ellicott catches the turn of the knife: "dealt proudly" is the word used of the Egyptians eight verses earlier, and the Hebrew of Exodus 18:11. Henry makes pride the root rather than a symptom — "pride is at the bottom of men's obstinacy and disobedience; they think it below them to bow their necks to God's yoke" — and names two failures of attention: they heard the word without hearkening and saw the works without being mindful, where weighing the wonders as miracles would have bred obedience from faith, as mercies from gratitude.

Verse 17 raises a textual question and a moral one. Clarke argues that bemiryam, "in their rebellion", is a copyist's error for bemitsrayim, "in Egypt", the reading of several manuscripts, the Septuagint, and Numbers 14:4. Ellicott concurs, noting that at Numbers the appointment is only proposed. Wesley closes that gap by intention rather than text: they resolved it, and are said to have done it "as Abraham is said to have offered up Isaac", because he intended to. Against the rebellion stands the title, which Henry and Ellicott both take from the margin as "a God of pardons". Gill traces the calf to Egypt too, an imitation of the Apis, and Henry pairs the apostasies as one backward glance — to Egyptian slavery for the garlick and onions, and to Egyptian idolatry.

Clarke distinguishes three postures of the cloud: a pillar going before to point the way, a pillar of fire by night for light and rallying, and an extended cloud hovering over the camp to refresh it with dews and shield it from the sun. On the good Spirit, Gill reports the Jewish readings, the spirit of prophecy or that put upon the seventy elders, while Ellicott notes that the Spirit's teaching function "occurs here only, and is a remarkable anticipation of the New Testament."

The conquest verses draw Clarke into another repair: "the land of Sihon, and the land of the king of Heshbon" names two kings where only one can be meant, so he renders the conjunction "even." Ellicott, seeing a deliberate double reference to the one king, corrects "divide them into corners" to dividing the nations unto Israel within their boundaries; Wesley keeps the corners and makes them social, the remnants cooped up town by town. Over the prosperity that followed, Clarke sets an old maxim, matched from Sallust: "war begets poverty, poverty begets peace, peace begets affluence, affluence begets luxury and corruption of manners; and hence civil broils, foreign wars, and desolations." Henry says the ruin was gratuitous: Canaan could not have made them happier, "had it not been their own fault."

For the cycle that follows, Clarke and Ellicott agree on the source: Judges is a history of God's mercies and Israel's rebellions, and its phraseology is remembered here. Henry presses that deliverance was never a verdict on the delivered — God gave them saviours "not for any merit of theirs, for they deserved nothing but ill" — and testified against their sins when he rescued them, lest they misconstrue deliverance as connivance at their wickedness. On the prophets he identifies the testimony as the Spirit's own, and draws a rule for ministry: bring people to God by bringing them to his law, "not to bring them to ourselves by bringing them under any law of ours." Clarke reads "many years" of the ten tribes, and takes "by thy Spirit in thy prophets" to give "the true notion of Divine inspiration." Gill renders the forbearance "thou didst draw upon them", which Jarchi takes of mercy drawn out of God's own heart. Keil and Delitzsch supply the limit verse 31 asserts: God did not suffer them to become extinct in exile but preserved a remnant. Henry states it as intent — "he did not stir up all his wrath, for he designed their reformation, not their destruction."
32:
"Here begins the prayer proper," says Ellicott. Gill hears Nehemiah's own voice in the titles — the great, the mighty and the terrible God are his opening chapter's words — and concludes that "the whole prayer is his composure, delivered by him to the Levites", against Ellicott's suggestion at verse 5 that the psalm may be Ezra's. Wesley explains why mercy is joined to covenant: it "was not a sufficient ground of hope, because they had so basely broken it. God was discharged from keeping it, and therefore they fly to God's free and rich mercy." Keil and Delitzsch put the plea in a sentence: that God not lightly regard the affliction, though kings and people had fully deserved it. Ellicott identifies the Assyrian kings as "the rod of God's anger" of Isaiah 10:5, from Pul to Esar-haddon, successive scourges; Clarke reads the roll of sufferers as a ladder descending from kings to the common people: "those who disturb this natural order (for it subsists even in Britain) are enemies to the peace of the whole."

The confession of verse 33 is unqualified. Gill grants they could not complain of any wrong, and that had God shown no mercy it was but what they deserved. Wesley makes it a rule: under rebukes of providence, "be they ever so sharp, or ever so long continued", it becomes us still to justify God and own that we are punished less than our iniquities deserve. Henry lays the guilt across every order — kings, princes, priests, fathers, "and we in them" — and finds the punishment shaped to the crime: those who would not serve God in their own land were made to serve enemies in a strange one, as Deuteronomy 28:47 had threatened.

Three readers notice one omission: the prophets, listed among the afflicted at verse 32, are absent from the transgressors at verse 34. Clarke says they were left out because "they continued faithful to God, testifying by his Spirit against the crimes of all, even at the risk of their lives"; Keil and Delitzsch, that as God's witnesses they are not reckoned among the offenders though they shared the affliction. On the next clause they part. Clarke prefers the variant bemalcuthecha, "in thy kingdom", found in Kennicott's manuscripts and the Septuagint, calling it "most likely to be the true reading"; Keil and Delitzsch keep "in their kingdom", meaning while the kingdom was still independent, and trace "the large and fat land" to Exodus 3:8.

What the distress consists in divides them sharply. Clarke takes it politically: tribute is exacted at the sovereign's pleasure, not by fixed rate, "so that we can neither call our persons, our time, our land, nor our cattle, our own" — "miserable are the people that live under such a government. Think of this, ye Britons!" Wesley keeps it domestic: "we plow, and sow, and labour, and thou givest thy blessing to our endeavours; and yet in a great measure this is not for ourselves." Ellicott moves it inward: the distress is "not so much under the Persian yoke as in the remembrance of God's judgments", the force of the passage lying in its comparison, almost word by word, of what the land was given for with what it has become. The levy on bodies and cattle, he notes, was military, and the priests do not exempt themselves from it.

Gill reads the closing formula with Jarchi as "in all this distress" rather than "because of all this". Ellicott supplies the mechanics of sealing — each party pressed his seal into moist clay — while Clarke reads the signatory list as constitutional evidence, a mixed aristocracy of nobles for the civil department, priests and Levites for the ecclesiastical: "this was not mixing the Church with the state, or the state with the Church: both were separate, yet both mutually supported each other."
